statement: A paper strip is folded in half, then in half again. One straight cut is made across it, through all the layers, away from the folds. How many pieces are there?

choices.misconception: I thought one straight cut always makes two pieces, however the paper was folded.
I thought folding in half twice makes only 2 layers, so the cut went through the strip in 2 places.
I worked out there are 4 layers, so the strip is cut in 4 places, but I forgot that 4 cuts make one more piece than cuts.
I thought each of the 4 layers is cut into 2 separate pieces, giving $4 \times 2 = 8$.

hints: How many layers of paper does the scissors go through?
Each fold in half doubles the layers. A cut through every layer cuts the unfolded strip in that many places. Then think of a straight strip cut in several places: how many pieces?
After two folds there are 4 layers, so the strip is cut in 4 places. Cutting a strip in 4 places gives one more piece than the number of cuts.

solutions.reliable: One fold in half makes 2 layers; folding again makes 4 layers. The cut goes through all 4 layers, so when the strip is opened it has been cut in 4 different places. A strip cut in 4 places falls into $4 + 1 = 5$ pieces. You can check with a real strip of paper: the three middle pieces each have a fold in them and the two end pieces do not. The transferable idea: count layers to count cuts, then remember that cuts in a strip make one more piece.
solutions.elegant: Small cases: no fold, one cut, 2 pieces. One fold gives 2 layers, 2 cuts, 3 pieces. Two folds give 4 layers, 4 cuts, 5 pieces. The pieces are always one more than the layers.

whyOnTest: Folding and cutting questions reward tracking layers rather than picturing the final shape, and the fence-post step catches the hasty.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
